blocks.content: Deadlock prevention takes a structural approach to a problem that could otherwise strike at any time. Instead of watching the system at runtime and reacting once trouble appears, prevention removes the danger before the system even starts, by making sure one of the four conditions a deadlock needs can never be true in the first place.

This chapter, part of the dedicated Deadlocks module, walks through the four prevention techniques, one for each of the four necessary conditions. Each technique guarantees deadlock is structurally impossible, but each also comes with a real cost. By the end you will be able to weigh those costs against each other, and understand why resource ordering, the technique that attacks circular wait, is the one used most often in production systems.

1. The Core Strategy: Make One Condition Impossible
blocks.text: 1. The Core Strategy: Make One Condition Impossible

blocks.content: Every deadlock, no matter how complicated the system, needs all four necessary conditions to hold at the same time: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Deadlock prevention exploits this fact directly. If the system is designed so that even one of these four conditions can never occur, structurally, by the rules of the system itself, then a deadlock becomes impossible, regardless of how many processes are running or in what order they happen to execute.

This is a strong guarantee, and it is the defining trait of prevention. Deadlock avoidance, covered in the next topic in this module, still allows all four conditions to exist in principle and instead watches each resource request carefully at runtime to steer the system around danger. Detection and recovery, covered later still, lets deadlocks happen and cleans up after the fact. Prevention is the only one of the three that removes the possibility entirely, before a single process even runs.

Because there are exactly four necessary conditions, there are exactly four corresponding prevention techniques, one aimed at each condition. A real system typically commits to a single technique for a given class of resources, since attacking a condition that was never going to hold anyway wastes effort. The rest of this chapter walks through each technique in turn, one section per condition.

blocks.title: One condition is enough
blocks.content: You do not need to defeat all four conditions to prevent deadlock. Structurally ruling out just one of them, for a given class of resources, is sufficient on its own, and no order of execution can ever produce a deadlock once that condition is gone.
2. Attacking Mutual Exclusion

The most direct way to remove a condition is to make it not apply at all. Mutual exclusion requires that at least one resource be held in a non shareable way, so if a resource can instead be made shareable, several processes can use it at once and there is nothing left to wait for. A read only copy of a file is a common example: if every process only needs to read data and never write it, handing out copies removes the exclusivity entirely, and no process ever blocks another over it.

Spooling is the classic version of this idea for physical devices. A printer can only physically print one document at a time, so instead of letting processes fight over direct, exclusive access to the printer itself, the operating system gives every process fast, non blocking access to a spool queue instead. Each process simply writes its print job into the queue, and a separate print daemon works through the queue in the background, one job at a time, without any process ever waiting on another process directly.

This technique has an honest limit. Not every resource can be made shareable, no matter how creative the design. A write lock on a database row, a device mid transaction, or any resource where two processes genuinely modifying it at once would corrupt the result, still needs exclusive access. Mutual exclusion prevention attacks the condition where it is possible to attack it, but it cannot eliminate the condition everywhere, which is exactly why the other three techniques exist.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408658947-293431076.png
3. Attacking Hold and Wait

Hold and wait describes a process that is already holding one resource while it waits for another. The prevention technique here targets that combination directly, most commonly by requiring a process to request every resource it will ever need for its entire run, all at once, up front, before it is allowed to start. The operating system either grants the complete set immediately or grants nothing at all, so a process is never caught holding one resource while blocked waiting for a second.

A second variant works from the other direction: a process that wants a new resource must first release every resource it currently holds, then request the full new set together. Either variant removes the possibility of a process simultaneously holding something and waiting for something else, which is exactly the condition being attacked.

The real downside is low resource utilization. A process that will eventually need ten different resources, but only actually touches each one briefly at different points in its execution, still has to acquire and hold all ten from the very start, leaving most of them sitting idle for long stretches while other processes cannot use them. There is also a starvation risk: a process that needs many resources, or an unusual combination of resources, may keep losing out to processes with smaller requests and simply never accumulate everything it needs at the same time.

blocks.title: Starvation risk
blocks.content: A process that always needs a large or unusual combination of resources can be repeatedly passed over in favor of processes with smaller requests, and may wait indefinitely even though no true deadlock exists.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408658947-567595824.png
4. Attacking No Preemption

No preemption means a resource can only be released voluntarily, by the process holding it, once that process finishes using it. This prevention technique removes that rule: the operating system is allowed to forcibly take a resource away from a process that holds it, typically by rolling that process back to an earlier safe state, releasing the resource it was preempted from, and letting another process that needs it proceed.

This is exactly how a modern operating system handles the processor itself. A running process can be interrupted at essentially any point, its register state saved, and the processor handed to another process, with the original resuming later as though nothing happened. Preemption of the processor happens so routinely that most programs never notice it at all.

The real downside is added complexity and the cost of rollback. Saving and restoring state safely is only clean for resources whose state can actually be captured and replayed, such as CPU registers or memory pages. It does not work cleanly for something like a printer halfway through an in progress print job, since there is no safe way to rewind a physical sheet of paper that has already been printed on. This technique works well for resources with recoverable state, and poorly for resources with physical, one way side effects.

5. Attacking Circular Wait

Circular wait is the condition where a chain of processes forms a cycle, each one waiting for a resource held by the next, until the chain loops back on itself. The prevention technique here imposes a strict, global numbering on every resource type in the system, and requires that every process request resources only in strictly increasing order of that number. A process holding resource number five is simply not allowed to turn around and request resource number two.

This works for a precise reason, not just an intuitive one. Picture any attempted cycle among processes: each process in the chain would need to be holding a lower numbered resource and requesting a higher numbered one, since that is the only kind of request the rule permits. But for the chain to close into a cycle, the very last process would need to request the resource held by the first process, and that resource must be lower numbered, since it is the one that started the chain. Requesting it would break the increasing order rule, so that final link in the cycle can never legally form. Without that last link there is no cycle, and without a cycle there is no circular wait.

Resource ordering is by a wide margin the most commonly used prevention technique in real systems. It is easy to implement, does not require declaring resources up front the way hold and wait prevention does, and does not need the rollback machinery that no preemption prevention requires. Many production codebases enforce it as a simple coding convention: always acquire locks in a fixed, agreed order, such as by memory address or by a lock ID assigned when the lock is created.

blocks.title: The most practical technique
blocks.content: Resource ordering attacks circular wait without touching resource sharing, without forcing processes to request everything up front, and without any rollback machinery. This is why it dominates in practice over the other three techniques.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408658948-905722624.png
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408658948-727210063.png

If every process must request resources in the same fixed order, the last process in any potential cycle would have to request an already lower numbered resource, which the rule forbids, so the cycle can never close.
6. Worked Example: Ordering the Two Thread Two Lock Scenario
blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: Ordering the Two Thread Two Lock Scenario

blocks.content: Recall the classic two thread, two lock deadlock. Thread A acquires Lock 1 and then tries to acquire Lock 2. Thread B acquires Lock 2 and then tries to acquire Lock 1. If the timing lines up so that Thread A grabs Lock 1 while Thread B grabs Lock 2, before either one requests its second lock, each thread ends up waiting forever for a lock the other is holding.

Resource ordering fixes this with a single rule: assign every lock a fixed number when it is created, and require every thread to acquire locks only in increasing numeric order. Say Lock 1 is numbered lower than Lock 2. Under the rule, Thread B is no longer allowed to acquire Lock 2 before Lock 1, it must request Lock 1 first, exactly like Thread A does.

With both threads following the same order, the worst case is no longer a deadlock, only ordinary blocking. If Thread A grabs Lock 1 first, Thread B simply waits at Lock 1 until Thread A finishes with both locks and releases them, and then Thread B proceeds normally. There is no longer any way for one thread to hold Lock 1 while waiting for Lock 2 at the same moment the other holds Lock 2 while waiting for Lock 1, because both threads now always request Lock 1 before Lock 2.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408658948-177215509.png

blocks.content: 7. Comparing the Four Prevention Techniques

Each of the four techniques guarantees the same outcome, deadlock becomes structurally impossible, but they reach it in very different ways and at very different costs. Seeing them side by side makes the tradeoffs, and the reason resource ordering is favored in practice, much clearer.

8. Why Prevention Is Not Always the Practical Choice
blocks.text: 8. Why Prevention Is Not Always the Practical Choice

blocks.content: Deadlock prevention gives an absolute guarantee, deadlock simply cannot happen, and that guarantee holds no matter what order processes run in or how loaded the system is. That certainty is valuable, but it is bought at a price. Every technique above either restricts how resources can be shared, forces processes to grab far more than they immediately need, or adds rollback machinery, and each of these choices tends to lower concurrency and shrink how efficiently the system uses its resources.

This is exactly why deadlock avoidance, the next topic in this dedicated Deadlocks module, is often preferred when it is feasible. Avoidance still allows all four necessary conditions to exist in the system, but it examines every resource request as it arrives and only grants requests that keep the system in a state from which every process can still finish. It trades the absolute, structural guarantee of prevention for better resource utilization, at the cost of needing more information about future requests and more computation at request time.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408658949-900384121.png
blocks.alt: Why Prevention Is Not Always the Practical Choice

blocks.content: 9. Common Mistakes

["Assuming any single prevention technique is free of tradeoffs. Every one of the four reduces concurrency, resource utilization, or flexibility somewhere, there is no free option.","Forgetting that resource ordering must be applied globally and consistently across the entire system, not just within one module or one team's code.","Letting a single process, or a single piece of legacy code, skip the agreed resource order. Even one process that ignores the rule can reintroduce circular wait and undo the guarantee for everyone else.","Mixing two different prevention techniques for the same resource without thinking it through, which can quietly reintroduce one of the four conditions through the back door."]
items: Assuming any single prevention technique is free of tradeoffs. Every one of the four reduces concurrency, resource utilization, or flexibility somewhere, there is no free option.
Forgetting that resource ordering must be applied globally and consistently across the entire system, not just within one module or one team's code.

Letting a single process, or a single piece of legacy code, skip the agreed resource order. Even one process that ignores the rule can reintroduce circular wait and undo the guarantee for everyone else.
Mixing two different prevention techniques for the same resource without thinking it through, which can quietly reintroduce one of the four conditions through the back door.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: If you can only prepare one prevention technique in depth, make it resource ordering. It is the technique most frequently used in real systems, from lock acquisition order in multi threaded code to lock ordering conventions inside database engines, and interviewers often use the two thread two lock scenario specifically to see whether you can explain why ordering breaks the cycle, not just that it does.
